masteryZone.q: Which of the following describes the key administrative change under 1. Centralization of Administration?
opts: The Governor-General of Bengal became the Governor-General of India
The Governor-General's Executive Council was reduced to 3 members
A bicameral central legislature was established in Calcutta
The system of dual government was created
masteryZone.sol: The Charter Act of 1833 elevated the Governor-General of Bengal to the post of the Governor-General of India, making Lord William Bentinck the first GGI.

masteryZone.q: Under the provisions of 1. Centralization of Administration, which presidency lost its independent legislative power?
opts: Madras Presidency only
Bombay Presidency only
Both Madras and Bombay Presidencies
Bengal Presidency only
masteryZone.sol: The Act completely stripped Bombay and Madras Presidencies of their legislative powers, vesting all legislative authority in GGI-in-Council.

masteryZone.q: Who was appointed as the first Law Member under the provisions of 1. Centralization of Administration?
opts: Lord Cornwallis
Lord Macaulay
Warren Hastings
Henry Dundas
masteryZone.sol: Lord Macaulay was appointed as the first Law Member (fourth member) of the Governor-General's Council in 1833.

masteryZone.q: What was EIC's modified status after the commercial provisions of 1. Centralization of Administration?
opts: It was completely dissolved and liquidating
It became a purely administrative body governing in trust for the Crown
It became a joint stock bank in Calcutta
It was given absolute monopoly over tea and China trade
masteryZone.sol: The Charter Act of 1833 terminated EIC's trade functions, transforming it into a purely administrative body acting as a trustee for the Crown.

masteryZone.q: Under the social reform guidelines of 1. Centralization of Administration, the council was directed to abolish which practice?
opts: Infanticide
Sati system
Slavery
Child marriage
masteryZone.sol: The Act directed the GGI-in-Council to mitigate and eventually abolish slavery in British India, leading to Act V of 1843.

masteryZone.q: Which of the following EIC monopolies were abolished by the Charter Act of 1833? (Select all that apply)
opts: Monopoly of trade in tea
Monopoly of trade with China
Commercial operations in Bengal
Right to govern territorial revenues
masteryZone.sol: The Charter Act of 1833 ended all remaining trade monopolies of EIC, including tea and China trade, ending all EIC commercial operations. However, EIC retained its right to govern and collect revenues as a trustee.

masteryZone.q: Identify the key legislative changes introduced under 1. Centralization of Administration: (Select all that apply)
opts: Creation of the office of the Law Member
Legislative supremacy of the GGI-in-Council
Deprivation of Madras and Bombay legislative powers
Designation of council laws as 'Regulations' instead of 'Acts'
masteryZone.sol: The Law Member was created, GGI-in-Council was made supreme, and Madras/Bombay lost legislative powers. Council laws were now called 'Acts', replacing 'Regulations'.

masteryZone.q: Which of the following statement(s) is/are correct regarding EIC civil service selection attempt in 1833? (Select all that apply)
opts: The Act proposed a system of open competition
Clause 87 barred EIC from debarring Indians from office based on religion or color
The open competition proposal was successfully implemented in 1833
Opposition from the Court of Directors blocked the open competition clause
masteryZone.sol: The Act proposed open competition and Clause 87 barred discrimination, but opposition from EIC Directors blocked the open competition proposal. It was only implemented in 1853.

masteryZone.q: What reforms were directed toward slavery and law codification under 1. Centralization of Administration? (Select all that apply)
opts: Mitigation and abolition of slavery in British India
Establishment of the first Law Commission in 1834
Codification of all Indian laws under Macaulay
Abolition of Sati system by GGI Macaulay
masteryZone.sol: Slavery mitigation, 1834 Law Commission, and codification under Lord Macaulay were part of the 1833 reforms. Sati abolition occurred earlier in 1829 under Bentinck.

masteryZone.q: Which of the following describes the GGI-in-Council's powers after the passage of 1. Centralization of Administration? (Select all that apply)
opts: Full civil and military authority over all British India
Sole authority to pass legislative Acts
Financial control over Madras and Bombay revenues
Complete independence from Board of Control supervision
masteryZone.sol: The GGI had supreme civil/military control, sole legislative authority, and financial centralization. GGI was still supervised by the Board of Control.

masteryZone.q: Explain the conceptual shift from 'Regulations' to 'Acts' under 2. End of Commercial Body & Civil Services Attempt.

masteryZone.q: Which of the following EIC monopolies were abolished by the Charter Act of 1833? (Select all that apply)
opts: Monopoly of trade in tea
Monopoly of trade with China
Commercial operations in Bengal
Right to govern territorial revenues
masteryZone.sol: The Charter Act of 1833 ended all remaining trade monopolies of EIC, including tea and China trade, ending all EIC commercial operations. However, EIC retained its right to govern and collect revenues as a trustee.

masteryZone.q: Identify the key legislative changes introduced under 3. Law Member, Codification & Slavery Abolition: (Select all that apply)

Legislative supremacy of the GGI-in-Council
Deprivation of Madras and Bombay legislative powers
Designation of council laws as 'Regulations' instead of 'Acts'
masteryZone.sol: The Law Member was created, GGI-in-Council was made supreme, and Madras/Bombay lost legislative powers. Council laws were now called 'Acts', replacing 'Regulations'.

masteryZone.q: Which of the following statement(s) is/are correct regarding EIC civil service selection attempt in 1833? (Select all that apply)

The open competition proposal was successfully implemented in 1833
Opposition from the Court of Directors blocked the open competition clause
masteryZone.sol: The Act proposed open competition and Clause 87 barred discrimination, but opposition from EIC Directors blocked the open competition proposal. It was only implemented in 1853.

masteryZone.q: What reforms were directed toward slavery and law codification under 3. Law Member, Codification & Slavery Abolition? (Select all that apply)

Establishment of the first Law Commission in 1834
Codification of all Indian laws under Macaulay
Abolition of Sati system by GGI Macaulay
masteryZone.sol: Slavery mitigation, 1834 Law Commission, and codification under Lord Macaulay were part of the 1833 reforms. Sati abolition occurred earlier in 1829 under Bentinck.

masteryZone.q: Which of the following describes the GGI-in-Council's powers after the passage of 3. Law Member, Codification & Slavery Abolition? (Select all that apply)

Complete independence from Board of Control supervision

masteryZone.q: How did the Act centralized legislative powers in British India?
masteryZone.sol: By depriving the Governors of Bombay and Madras of their legislative capacities and vesting sole legislative authority in GGI-in-Council.

masteryZone.q: Imagine the Governor of Madras tries to pass an independent Regulation regarding local land revenue judicial courts in 1834. Evaluate the validity of this regulation under 3. Law Member, Codification & Slavery Abolition.
masteryZone.sol: This regulation is invalid. The Charter Act of 1833 stripped Bombay and Madras of their legislative powers, meaning Madras could no longer pass regulations. All laws had to be drafted as proposals and passed by the GGI-in-Council.

masteryZone.q: Explain the conceptual shift from 'Regulations' to 'Acts' under 3. Law Member, Codification & Slavery Abolition.
masteryZone.sol: Before 1833, legislations made by presidency councils were called 'Regulations'. With the creation of the Governor-General of India as the sole legislative authority for all territories, legislations made by GGI-in-Council were styled as 'Acts', representing uniform, sovereign law.
